newsitem.title: GABON: Ballot booths smashed in Gabon poll, vote extended.
newsitem.headline: Ballot booths smashed in Gabon poll, vote extended.

text.p: Angry voters smashed polling booths in central Gabon and held an official hostage as local elections in the oil producing country on Sunday degenerated into chaos, election officials said.
Authorities acknowledging organisational problems decided to extend voting indefinitely after the 6 p.m. (1700 GMT) official close. Officials said people could still be voting by midnight.
"The polls will stay open for as long as it takes for everyone to be able to vote," a senior official of the National Election Commission told Reuters.
The municipal elections are intended to test a 1994 deal between the government and the opposition, defuse sometimes bloody political rivalry and set its democratic transition back on course.
Troops backed by tanks took up positions in the sidestreets of Libreville. State television showed newsfilm of irate voters unable to cast their ballots smashing polling stations in Libreville.
"The election is completely chaotic. They started smashing the booths at Fougamou," National Election Committee vice-president Mengome Atome told Reuters.
Atome said a polling official had been held hostage in his office in Port Gentil, the hub of the Central African country's oil industry.
"Our officials said he had been taken hostage after voting collapsed," Atome said. There were no other details.
Radio stations reported that polling stations in Port Gentil had also been attacked.

Several hours after polls opened officially at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT), people headed back home as most polling stations had no ballots, voter lists or even officials. Many polling stations did not open until afternoon.

"The problem is not so much political as organisational," the election commission's Atome said. The commission had only 10 days to organise voting, enter all the names into the computer and hand out voter cards, he added.
The electoral commission is based in the grounds of the Republican Guard, formerly the Presidential Guard. Opposition critics say this does not bode well for the neutrality of the election results.
More than 12,000 candidates stood for election as councillors or mayors in the nine provinces of the former French colony.

There was confusion in the runup to the poll about the number of people who would be able to vote in the nation of just 1.2 million people. Voter registration ended on October 17 but election officials said computer generation of 400,000 registration and voting cards was behind schedule.
